extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, researchers and activists interested in comparative blasphemy law and freedom of expression
extracted.subtask_description: A comparative encyclopedia-style summary of national and regional laws, prosecutions, and legal standards criminalising or regulating blasphemy, religious insult, sacrilege, or protection of religious feelings across many countries and jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poland — criminalisation of offending religious feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: Law criminalising 'offending religious feelings' (used by politicians and activists to prosecute perceived offences; convictions include fines and possible restriction of liberty up to 2 years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The provision has been criticised as vague and abused to limit freedom of speech and debate about Church crimes and influence. Notable convictions: Dorota 'Doda' Rabczewska fined 5,000 zł; Jerzy Urban fined 120,000 zł for publishing an image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Romania — prohibition on cults infringing fundamental rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Romanian law: 'cults, religious associations and religious groups ... must not infringe upon ... fundamental human rights and liberties' (Constitution protects freedom of conscience and expression).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No active blasphemy law historically; administrative bodies (CNCD) have fined cultural institutions for works described as 'obscenity', 'mockery', 'blasphemy', 'sacrilege' (example: Nymphs & Zombies exhibition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Russia — Article 148 criminalising public disrespect of believers' feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 148: crime to conduct 'public actions expressing explicit disrespect for society and committed for the purpose of offending the religious feelings of believers'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part 2 imposes stricter punishments when such actions are coupled with desecration of holy symbols and/or religious texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seychelles — Section 128 'wounding religious feelings'
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 128 of the Seychelles Penal Code criminalises 'wounding religious feelings' with a penalty of imprisonment for a year.

rubrics_metrics.name: South Africa — common law blasphemy vs. Equality Act limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Blasphemy is a common law offence defined as 'unlawfully, intentionally and publicly acting contemptuously towards God.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some argue the offence is unconstitutional after the 1994 Bill of Rights. The Equality Act 2000 forbids hate speech (words based on prohibited grounds such as religion) and provides civil, not criminal, penalties for speech that is 'hurtful', 'harmful' or 'promote/propagate hatred.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Spain — Article 525 'vilification' of religious feelings/dogmas
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 525 of the Spanish Penal Code considers 'vilification' of religious 'feelings', 'dogmas', 'beliefs' or 'rituals'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This has been used in practice in cases against artists; critics view the provision as functionally close to a blasphemy law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sweden — no explicit blasphemy prohibition; 'agitation against a specific group' protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Swedish law does not explicitly prohibit blasphemy; instead, an Act on 'agitation against a specific group of people' protects minority groups sharing 'race, skin colour, national or ethnic origin, faith or sexual orientation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Act protects practitioners (people) rather than religions as such; enforcement has been applied against actions (e.g., Quran burnings) that constitute agitation against a specific group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Switzerland — Article 261 'Attack on the freedom of faith and the freedom to worship'
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 261: 'Any person who publicly and maliciously insults or mocks the religious convictions of others ... or maliciously desecrates objects of religious veneration ... or maliciously prevents, disrupts or publicly mocks an act of worship ... shall be liable to a monetary penalty.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text framed as protection of freedom of worship; penalty is monetary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tanzania (mainland) — sacrilege and wounding religious feelings (Articles 125, 129)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mainland Penal Code criminalises acts of sacrilege (destroying, damaging or defiling buildings or objects 'held sacred by any class of persons') and uttering words with intent to wound religious feelings under Articles 125 and 129; both are misdemeanours punishable by up to one year imprisonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforcement information is limited; Zanzibar (semi-autonomous) has similar provisions with separate penalties under its Penal Decree Act 2004 (Article 117 sacrilege; Article 121 uttering words with intent to wound).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tuvalu — Section 127 'wounding religious feelings'
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 127 of the Tuvalu Penal Code criminalises 'wounding religious feelings' with a penalty of imprisonment for a year.

rubrics_metrics.name: United Kingdom — historic common law blasphemy and abolition
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically, common law offences of blasphemy existed in the UK (England & Wales, Scotland). England & Wales abolished common law blasphemy and blasphemous libel in 2008; Scotland decriminalised blasphemy 2021 (common law offence abolished from 1 April 2024). Northern Ireland still had common law offences though unused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court rulings limited application (e.g., stage productions and broadcasts excluded under Theatres Act 1968 s.2(4) and Broadcasting Act 1990 s.6). Law Commission (1985) recommended abolition without replacement.

rubrics_metrics.name: British Virgin Islands & Montserrat — public use of abusive/blasphemous language
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 289 (BVI Criminal Code 1997) and Section 325 (Montserrat Penal Code) criminalise 'abusive, blasphemous, indecent, insulting, profane or threatening language' in a public place, punishable by up to three months imprisonment or a fine up to US$250.

rubrics_metrics.name: United States — Joseph Burstyn precedent limiting state censorship of 'sacrilegious' content
rubrics_metrics.description: In Joseph Burstyn, Inc. v. Wilson (1952), the U.S. Supreme Court ruled New York could not enforce a censorship law against films containing 'sacrilegious' content, holding the state has no legitimate interest in protecting religions from views distasteful to them sufficient to justify prior restraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an important First Amendment precedent protecting expression with religiously offensive content from state censorship prior restraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: United States (Pennsylvania) — corporate name restriction struck down
rubrics_metrics.description: Pennsylvania had an incorporation provision (enacted 1977) forbidding corporations from names that 'constitute blasphemy, profane cursing or swearing, or that profane the Lord's name'; this provision was found unconstitutional in 2010 in litigation by a filmmaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrates that some blasphemy-related statutes have been invalidated on constitutional grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: United States — sentencing enhancement for bias-motivated offenses (USSG §3A1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: US Sentencing Guidelines §3A1.1: if the factfinder determines beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant intentionally selected a victim or property because of actual or perceived religion (among other protected characteristics), the sentencing court must increase the standard sentencing range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a penalty enhancement for bias motivation rather than a stand-alone blasphemy offence.

rubrics_metrics.name: General — Islamic-derived normative views on blasphemy
rubrics_metrics.description: In many Muslim-majority countries, values and attitudes derived from Islam have influenced laws criminalising blasphemy; 'blasphemy' in Islam is broadly defined as impious utterance or action concerning God, Muhammad or anything considered sacred in Islam. The Quran admonishes blasphemy but does not specify punishment; some hadiths suggest punishments including death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical penalties vary widely by country and interpretation of Sharia; applied by state law or by extra-judicial vigilantism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Afghanistan — Sharia-based prohibition with capital punishment possible
rubrics_metrics.description: An Islamic emirate, Afghanistan prohibits blasphemy under Sharia; blasphemy can be punished by retaliatory penalties up to and including execution by hanging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since the Taliban takeover in 2021 people have been arrested for blasphemy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algeria — penal sanctions for blasphemy
rubrics_metrics.description: Although Algeria is predominantly Sunni Muslim and Islam is the state religion, Algeria uses retaliatory legislation rather than Sharia to combat blasphemy. The penalty can be up to 5 years imprisonment and a fine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bangladesh — prohibition on 'hurting religious sentiments'
rubrics_metrics.description: Bangladesh forbids blasphemy by a penal code provision that prohibits 'hurting religious sentiments', and by other laws and policies that limit freedom of speech; government has resisted calls for death penalty but retains laws dealing with hurting religious sentiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to limit speech; political pressure can influence enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Egypt — Article 98(f) Penal Code criminalising religiously charged extreme ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 98(f): confinement 6 months to 5 years, or fine 500–1,000 pounds for whoever makes use of religion in propagating, by words or writing or other means, extreme ideas for the purpose of inciting strife, ridiculing or insulting a heavenly religion or a sect following it, or damaging national unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targets propagation of 'extreme ideas' and protection of 'national unity'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indonesia — Article 156(a) forbidding public hostility/ contempt towards religion
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 156(a) Criminal Code forbids anyone from deliberately, in public, expressing feelings of hostility, hatred, or contempt against religions with the purpose of preventing others from adhering to any religion, and forbids anyone from disgracing a religion; penalty maximum five years imprisonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in high-profile prosecutions (e.g., Basuki Tjahaja Purnama).

rubrics_metrics.name: Iran — blasphemy laws derived from Sharia and state rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Iran, an Islamic theocracy, derives its law against blasphemy from Sharia; laws against blasphemy complement laws against criticizing the government, insulting Islam, and publishing materials that deviate from Islamic standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application is within a broader framework of religiously-informed restrictions on expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jordan — Articles 273 and 278 penalising scorn of Prophets and insulting religious beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 273 criminalises 'scorning or reviling any of the Prophets' with imprisonment up to three years; Article 278 criminalises 'publishing anything that would insult the religious feelings or religious beliefs of other people.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Kuwait — cybercrime punishment for insulting sacred figures (Article 6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 6 of Kuwait's cybercrime laws prescribes punishment of up to 12 months in prison and a 20,000 KWD fine for insulting 'God, the Holy Quran, Prophets, the Noble Companions of Prophet Muhammad, Wives of the Prophet, or persons who are part of the Prophet's family.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targets online/digital expressions specifically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Malaysia — multi-layered protections against insulting religion
rubrics_metrics.description: Malaysia prevents insult to religion via education, broadcasting/publishing restrictions, and legal system; some states operate Sharia courts to protect Islam and the Malaysian Penal Code provides penalties for offences against religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framework includes both civil/regulatory media controls and criminal penalties via federal and state law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mauritania — apostasy and repentance provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Mauritania's Penal Code (Act of Indecency toward Islam) defines apostasy procedures: Article 306(1) indicates every Muslim guilty of apostasy will be invited to repent within three days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows criminal/legal framework for apostasy within broader blasphemy/indecency provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nigeria — section 204 and Sharia courts; risk of vigilantism
rubrics_metrics.description: Nigeria prohibits blasphemy by section 204 of the Criminal Code and permits Sharia courts to operate in some states; enforcement is complicated by frequent vigilantism that can usurp courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rights and enforcement vary across federal and state/Sharia jurisdictions; violent extra-judicial responses are common.

rubrics_metrics.name: Northern Cyprus — criminalised but rarely enforced
rubrics_metrics.description: U.S. Department of State reports that blasphemy is criminalised in Northern Cyprus, but the law is rarely enforced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pakistan — Chapter XV, Sections 295–298C and death penalty under §295-C
rubrics_metrics.description: Pakistan's Penal Code contains numerous provisions: §295 injuring/defiling place of worship; §295‑A deliberate and malicious acts intended to outrage religious feelings; §295‑B defiling the Holy Qur'an; §295‑C derogatory remarks re the Holy Prophet; §296 disturbing religious assembly; §297 trespassing on burial places; §298 uttering words with deliberate intent to wound religious feelings; §298‑A/B/C various protections. There is a death penalty for blasphemy under §295‑C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prosecutions disproportionately affect minorities (Ahmadiyya, Christians) and accused persons, police, lawyers and judges may face harassment, threats, attacks and murder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Palestine — military/civil provisions for incitement and insulting religious leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: Palestinian National Authority uses civil and military law provisions: charges have included 'inciting religious hatred' (Article 177), 'insulting religious leaders' (Articles 225 and 226/B), and 'offending religious views' (Article 230/A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases have involved online criticism and led to detention and prosecution under older Jordanian statutes in the West Bank.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qatar — imprisonment and fines for blasphemy and defamatory imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Qatar: penalty for blasphemy is a jail sentence of up to seven years; law also stipulates one-year prison sentence or QR1,000 fine for defamation of Islam by producing or promoting defamatory imagery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious criticism on websites is censored; blasphemy accusations can be treated as evidence of apostasy (which can carry the death penalty in some interpretations) though no apostasy punishment has been recorded since 1971.

rubrics_metrics.name: Saudi Arabia — Sharia/royal edicts/fatawa prescribe severe penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: Saudi Arabia mixes Sharia, royal edicts, and fatawa to prescribe penalties for blasphemy, including up to the death penalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws are enforced in a theocratic framework with limited procedural protections noted in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sudan — Section 125 criminalising insulting religion with corporal penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 125 of the Sudanese Criminal Act prohibits 'insulting religion, inciting hatred and showing contempt for religious beliefs' with penalties including imprisonment, a fine, and up to forty lashes. Notable cases include the 'teddy bear' blasphemy case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sudan repealed its apostasy law (Article 126) in July 2020 but blasphemy law (Article 125) remained under scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turkey — Article 216 (provoking rancour / humiliating / disrespecting religious belief)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 216: (1) openly provoking a group to be rancorous or hostile punished by 1–3 years if it causes risk to public safety; (2) openly humiliating another because of religion/social class punishable by 6 months–1 year; (3) openly disrespecting the religious belief of a group punishable by 6 months–1 year if such act causes potential risk for public peace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Has been used in prosecutions for social media posts; convictions have sometimes been reversed on appeal as within freedom of thought/expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: United Arab Emirates — Article 312 enumerated religious offences
rubrics_metrics.description: UAE Penal Code Article 312: public offences subject to at least one year imprisonment or fine include offence to any Islamic sacred beliefs or rites; insult to any of the divine recognized religions; approving/encouraging or promoting sinful actions; knowingly eating pork meat by Muslims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penalises both insulting religions and certain conduct considered sinful for Muslims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yemen — Sharia-based prosecutions and vigilante risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Accusations of blasphemy in Yemen are often aimed at minorities, intellectuals, artists, reporters and human rights defenders; the accused are subject to Islamic law (Sharia), and some interpretations prescribe death for blasphemy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unsourced claims in this section note extrajudicial violence and exile; enforcement is often harsh and dangerous for the accused.

rubrics_metrics.name: China — state censorship and banning works offensive to Islam or minorities
rubrics_metrics.description: China (officially an atheist state) has banned books and detained authors when material allegedly insulted Islam (example: 1989 book Xing Fengsu banned and authors arrested after protests); state media have advocated limiting freedom of speech in response to events like Charlie Hebdo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforcement and state responses can reflect sensitivities to minority protests and government control over expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Israel — Articles 170 and 173 (insult to religion; injury to religious sentiment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 170 (Insult to religion): destroying/desecrating place of worship or object held sacred with intention of reviling religion liable to three years' imprisonment. Article 173 (Injury to religious sentiment): publishing a publication liable to crudely offend religious faith or voicing in a public place words liable to crudely offend the religious faith of others is liable to one year's imprisonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These laws are rarely enforced but have led to some prosecutions and convictions in high-profile instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: India — Section 295A (deliberate and malicious outrage of religious feelings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 295A of the Indian Penal Code criminalises 'deliberate and malicious intention of outraging religious feelings' to prevent 'hate speech that insults or attempts to insult the religion or the religious beliefs' of any class of citizen; introduced in 1927 to maintain public order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires deliberate and malicious intention (distinguishing it from older English common law); widely used to prevent discussion and remains a threat to freedom of expression.
